raw_record.original_question:
A thermally conductive cylinder with smooth inner walls and a cross-sectional area of \( S \) is placed horizontally. At the exact midpoint of the cylinder, there are two small opposing baffles \( A \) and \( B \). Inside the cylinder, an ideal gas at temperature \( T_{0} \) is enclosed by a piston of negligible thickness and mass \( M \). The length of the cylinder is \( 2l \), the gravitational acceleration is \( g \), and the atmospheric pressure is \( p_{0} \). The cylinder is then slowly rotated clockwise until its opening faces vertically upward. There is no friction between the piston and the cylinder walls, and \( p_{0}S > M g \).

1. What is the height by which the piston descends during this process?
2. What is the pressure of the gas inside the cylinder when the temperature of the gas is reduced to $\frac{T_{0}}{2}$?
raw_record.final_cot:
First describe the image: The figure shows a horizontal cylinder, with a movable piston at the left end and mass M marked beside it; the gas is located on the right side of the piston and occupies the inside of the cylinder. The total length of the cylinder is marked as two equal segments l and l, so the total length is 2l. At the very middle position of the cylinder there are two opposite small stops, labeled A above and B below.

Then reason: Initially the cylinder is horizontal, and the piston's gravity is along the vertical direction and has no component along the cylinder axis; the piston is frictionless and the outside is at atmospheric pressure p0, so the initial pressure of the gas is p0. The initial gas volume is V0 = 2lS.

After the cylinder is slowly rotated clockwise until the opening is vertically upward, the piston is above the gas, and the gas is below the piston. The piston is subject to the external atmospheric pressure p0S and its own gravity Mg downward, and to the gas pressure pS upward. The equilibrium condition is pS = p0S + Mg, so p = p0 + Mg/S. Since the cylinder conducts heat and the process is slow, the rotation process can be regarded as an isothermal process, and the temperature is still T0; thus pV = constant: p0·2lS = (p0 + Mg/S)V. Solving gives the gas length after being turned vertical as L = V/S = 2lp0S/(p0S + Mg). The height by which the piston descends from the upper end is h = 2l - L = 2l - 2lp0S/(p0S + Mg) = 2Mgl/(p0S + Mg).

Continue to lower the gas temperature to T0/2. Since p0S > Mg, L = 2lp0S/(p0S + Mg) > l, so after being turned vertical the piston has not yet reached the midpoint stops. During cooling, the piston first moves downward under the external pressure p0S + Mg until it reaches the midpoint stops A and B, at which time the gas volume is lS. The temperature when it reaches the stops is higher than T0/2, so when it continues to cool to T0/2, the stops fix the piston and the gas volume remains lS. Using the initial amount of substance nR T0 = p0·2lS, with final temperature T0/2 and volume lS, the final pressure is p' = nR(T0/2)/(lS) = p0.

ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A thermally conductive cylinder with smooth inner walls and a cross-sectional area of \( S \) is placed horizontally. At the exact midpoint of the cylinder, there are two small opposing baffles \( A \) and \( B \). Inside the cylinder, an ideal gas at temperature \( T_{0} \) is enclosed by a piston of negligible thickness and mass \( M \). The length of the cylinder is \( 2l \), the gravitational acceleration is \( g \), and the atmospheric pressure is \( p_{0} \). The cylinder is then slowly rotated clockwise until its opening faces vertically upward. There is no friction between the piston and the cylinder walls, and \( p_{0}S > M g \).

1. What is the height by which the piston descends during this process?
2. What is the pressure of the gas inside the cylinder when the temperature of the gas is reduced to $\frac{T_{0}}{2}$?

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
First describe the image: The figure shows a horizontal cylinder, with a movable piston at the left end and mass M marked beside it; the gas is located on the right side of the piston and occupies the inside of the cylinder. The total length of the cylinder is marked as two equal segments l and l, so the total length is 2l. At the very middle position of the cylinder there are two opposite small stops, labeled A above and B below.

Then reason: Initially the cylinder is horizontal, and the piston's gravity is along the vertical direction and has no component along the cylinder axis; the piston is frictionless and the outside is at atmospheric pressure p0, so the initial pressure of the gas is p0. The initial gas volume is V0 = 2lS.

After the cylinder is slowly rotated clockwise until the opening is vertically upward, the piston is above the gas, and the gas is below the piston. The piston is subject to the external atmospheric pressure p0S and its own gravity Mg downward, and to the gas pressure pS upward. The equilibrium condition is pS = p0S + Mg, so p = p0 + Mg/S. Since the cylinder conducts heat and the process is slow, the rotation process can be regarded as an isothermal process, and the temperature is still T0; thus pV = constant: p0·2lS = (p0 + Mg/S)V. Solving gives the gas length after being turned vertical as L = V/S = 2lp0S/(p0S + Mg). The height by which the piston descends from the upper end is h = 2l - L = 2l - 2lp0S/(p0S + Mg) = 2Mgl/(p0S + Mg).

Continue to lower the gas temperature to T0/2. Since p0S > Mg, L = 2lp0S/(p0S + Mg) > l, so after being turned vertical the piston has not yet reached the midpoint stops. During cooling, the piston first moves downward under the external pressure p0S + Mg until it reaches the midpoint stops A and B, at which time the gas volume is lS. The temperature when it reaches the stops is higher than T0/2, so when it continues to cool to T0/2, the stops fix the piston and the gas volume remains lS. Using the initial amount of substance nR T0 = p0·2lS, with final temperature T0/2 and volume lS, the final pressure is p' = nR(T0/2)/(lS) = p0.
